claims.text: Rapid formation and self-healing of a passivating oxide film governs concurrent wear and corrosion resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys.
A nanocrystalline, high-entropy-stabilized matrix impedes crack propagation.
The passivating oxide film impedes penetration of corrosive ions.
The proposed initial microstructure is a fine-grained nanocrystalline BCC solid solution containing minor secondary phases such as Laves phases.
Minor Laves phases promote a high density of robust grain boundaries.
A high density of grain boundaries acts as a barrier to crack propagation.
Grain boundaries provide sites for rapid and uniform passivation.
Mechanical wear intermittently removes the protective surface layer.
The alloy composition and fine-grained structure enable rapid re-passivation after mechanical removal of the surface film.
The regenerated oxide film reduces wear by lowering friction and preventing direct metal-to-metal contact.
The regenerated oxide film reduces corrosion by acting as a chemical barrier.
Relative to a compositionally similar coarse-grained baseline, the refined alloy will have a lower combined wear-corrosion degradation rate.
Relative to the baseline, the refined alloy will have a lower wear rate and reduced wear-track depth during simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
Relative to the baseline, the refined alloy will show less pitting or a lower corrosion current density during simultaneous wear-corrosion testing.
The conventionally processed coarse-grained baseline has less effective re-passivation dynamics than the refined alloy.
The predicted advantage holds only when oxide-film regeneration is at least as rapid as mechanical removal.
The proposed mechanism may fail when abrasive loss outpaces film regeneration or when the environment inhibits oxide formation.
